target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally valuable because it is usually done with already-deceased animals or meat-industry byproducts, and that this does not meaningfully harm nature.
objection: Dissection animals are often obtained through harmful supply practices—AG2 says roughly 99% are caught in the wild—so animal dissection contributes to local population decline and biodiversity loss rather than being ethically neutral.

target: AG1’s idea that dissection is necessary because it is a valuable biology teaching method.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology or NGSS, and medical training in the U.S. and Canada does not use animals for physician preparation, so it is not needed for the curriculum or professional training.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection offers learning that alternatives cannot match.
objection: Synthetic models, virtual simulations, and computer-based labs can teach anatomy just as effectively or better, while avoiding dead animals and the harms of wild collection.

target: AG2’s claim that most classroom specimens are wild-caught and therefore cause biodiversity harm.
objection: That framing is said to be inaccurate for classroom use because most specimens are already dead and many come from food-production byproducts, so dissection does not create the biodiversity pressure AG2 claims.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives are enough because they can teach anatomy.
objection: Even if alternatives cover anatomy, they do not fully replicate the learning from real anatomical variability and hands-on inspection of actual structures, so simulations cannot fully replace dissection.

target: AG2’s implication that dissection is not practical or equitable in schools.
objection: Dissection can be a relatively low-cost, high-impact lab option for schools that cannot afford extensive virtual equipment, so it can increase access to hands-on biology rather than reduce it.

target: AG1’s defense of using already-dead/byproduct specimens as ethically acceptable.
objection: Even if specimens are already dead or from food chains, schools still create educational demand for animal bodies, which can increase breeding or wild collection in practice; available animals do not make the practice ethical when non-animal alternatives exist.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s authenticity and variability justify it.
objection: Good alternatives are based on real anatomy too, so students can learn structure and variation without sharps, biohazards, or disposal harms.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a worthwhile hands-on lab despite safety concerns.
objection: Dissection brings concrete safety and environmental downsides, including fixation chemicals, biohazard handling, and sharps disposal, which make it a worse educational choice than non-animal methods that avoid those harms.

target: AG2’s claim that educational demand for dissection animals increases animal death or biodiversity harm.
objection: Because most specimens are already dead and many are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, using them for class repurposes existing material instead of meaningfully increasing hunting or biodiversity loss.

target: AG2’s claim that safety/environmental problems make dissection a bad option.
objection: Safety and disposal risks are manageable through standard lab protocols, PPE, and regulated disposal, so those harms do not outweigh the tactile, real-anatomy learning value.

target: AG1’s reliance on byproduct/already-dead sourcing as a justification.
objection: Being a byproduct or already dead does not answer the ethical issue, because schools are still creating demand for animal death for an educational experience that could be achieved without killing animals.

target: AG1’s claim that proper protocols control the harms of dissection.
objection: Protocols do not remove the environmental and safety impacts, such as hazardous chemicals and regulated waste; compared with non-animal labs, dissection adds unnecessary risk and waste.

target: AG1’s sourcing claims about landfill-bound byproducts.
objection: Schools cannot reliably verify that specimens are truly waste products rather than animals from supply chains influenced by education demand, so the ethical sourcing claim is uncertain.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches unique learning goals better or in a distinct way.
objection: Alternatives may teach the same learning goals without animal bodies, so the burden is on dissection to justify itself; merely saying it has a distinct experience does not prove it is necessary.

target: AG1’s claim that repurposing byproduct animals makes dissection ethically acceptable.
objection: Even if animals would otherwise be discarded, the educational use still creates demand for animal death or animal bodies, which is avoidable if the same goals can be met without them.

target: AG1’s assertion that dissection can be made equitable through opt-outs and alternatives.
objection: Opt-outs do not solve the inclusion problem because dissection is often treated as the main or real lab, which can pressure students to participate or make alternatives feel second-best and stigmatizing.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is worth it because it uses already-deceased/byproduct animals and can be safety-managed.
objection: Even with regulated sourcing and safety, dissection still creates avoidable harms—chemicals, sharps, and biohazard waste—when alternatives can replace it.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out alternatives and dissection can be equally framed and graded.
objection: If the alternatives are truly equivalent, then dissection is not necessary; if dissection is uniquely high-impact, then opt-out students are not getting the same experience, so the arrangement still creates pressure and inequity.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a low-tech, cost-effective option for resource-limited schools.
objection: Dissection has recurring costs and burdens—specimen procurement, storage, fixatives, sharps disposal, and PPE—whereas reusable non-animal tools can be a more economical long-term choice.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a distinct learning route that can coexist with equivalent opt-outs.
objection: Dissection still requires handling real animal bodies and creating hazardous waste; because non-animal methods can meet the objectives without those harms, dissection is unnecessary even if alternatives are offered.

target: AG1’s claim that its dissection/opt-out model can preserve inclusion and equivalent learning.
objection: If the alternatives are truly equivalent, then dissection is optional and not needed; if dissection is uniquely valuable, then opt-out students are not really learning the same thing and may still be pressured or stigmatized.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely trains scientific practices such as observation, measurement, and troubleshooting.
objection: Those scientific skills do not require cutting up animals; non-animal methods can teach observation, data collection, labeling, documentation, and safety procedures without animal bodies.

target: AG1’s claim that real tissue is necessary for 3D spatial learning and that models cannot fully reproduce it.
objection: High-quality 3D models and virtual dissections can teach the same spatial relationships, often more carefully and repeatedly than a one-time dissection where cuts can obscure anatomy.

target: AG1’s stewardship framing that using byproduct bodies is ethically positive.
objection: Even if specimens are byproducts, dissection is still an educational choice that selects dead animals and creates waste and sharps handling when non-animal alternatives could meet the same goals.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is a distinct, high-value method rather than a replaceable option.
objection: Education is not binary, and alternatives can achieve the same biology outcomes; therefore dissection’s distinctiveness is not enough to justify animal use.

target: AG1’s claim that real tissue constraints improve learning.
objection: Dissection can be destructive and irreversible, and it may reward cutting technique more than conceptual understanding, while virtual or model-based alternatives can keep structures visible and support more reliable learning.

target: AG1’s claim that well-designed dissection is educational enough to justify itself.
objection: Even if dissection can teach, it is still unnecessary for AP/NGSS-aligned learning and for medical education, so the ethical justification must be stronger than merely showing that it works.

target: AG1’s suggestion that good instructional design makes animal dissection justified.
objection: Because the same learning objectives can be met with non-animal, repeatable methods, the harms of animal death, hazardous chemicals, sharps, and waste are avoidable, so dissection fails a proportionality test.
